task.goal: Make a small street-fair quiet zone useful without separating visitors by disability label.
hard_constraints: One tent, two volunteers and paper signs; no extra staff or permanent structure.
Access must be voluntary and available to anyone; no collection of diagnoses.
Compare use, crowd spillover and volunteer effort over two afternoons.
task.expected_result: A dignified quiet-space layout and trial.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use the site layout to shelter a quiet pocket
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is reducing exposure to passing crowds through tent placement, orientation and seating. Use the site plan to identify a permitted location away from speakers and queues, while keeping the tent visible from a main route. Face the entrance away from the busiest flow and arrange existing seats toward the quieter outlook, leaving a clear, accessible entrance and turning space. Paper signs at the approach and entrance say: “Quiet rest space — everyone welcome. Come and go freely.” Do not identify users by disability or ask why they enter.

One volunteer welcomes visitors without requiring conversation; the other monitors the approach and redirects fair queues that obstruct access. Both can support visitors when needed. The proposal assumes organizers permit repositioning the tent and that the site offers a meaningfully quieter orientation. A tent provides little sound insulation, so placement may offer only modest relief. Avoid hidden corners, blocked sightlines and locations that make the space hard to find.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across both afternoons, alternate comparable observation periods between ordinary perimeter seating and the sheltered orientation, keeping the welcome signs and available seats constant. Reconfigure only when visitors have left voluntarily. Volunteers record anonymous entry totals, occupied-seat snapshots, instances of people or queues obstructing the approach, and minutes spent welcoming, redirecting or rearranging. Offer an optional spoken question: “Was this restful enough?” No personal information is recorded. The mechanism is doubtful if the sheltered arrangement produces no clearer reports of relief while increasing access obstructions or volunteer effort. Record nearby performances and weather changes; this small trial cannot reliably separate their effects.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make quiet a shared activity rather than an identity
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is a clear, universal agreement about behavior inside the tent. A welcoming sign reads: “Quiet break — open to everyone. Please pause conversations and silence phone audio. No need to explain your visit.” Visitors may leave whenever they wish. This defines the space by what people do there, with no disability label or eligibility judgment.

Arrange existing seats with generous passage space and several seating directions so conversation is optional. One volunteer offers a brief welcome when useful; the second monitors the boundary and suggests that conversations continue outside the entrance, away from the access route. Use gentle reminders, never demands that distressed visitors suppress involuntary sounds. The space promises reduced conversation and amplified audio, not complete silence.

This requires visitors to understand and mostly follow the signs, and volunteers to feel comfortable making respectful reminders. It will have limited value if nearby music dominates the sound or if reminders themselves become intrusive. Use the existing tent, seating and paper signs only.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During each of two afternoons, alternate comparable periods using a general “Rest space — everyone welcome” sign and the explicit quiet agreement, keeping location and seating unchanged. Assume an ordinary clock is available for equal observation periods. Record entries, occupied-seat snapshots, audible conversations or phone audio, conversations displaced into the entrance route, and volunteer minutes and reminder counts. Ask willing departing visitors whether they could rest comfortably, without asking about diagnoses. The agreement is not supported if disruptive sound remains similar, or any improvement comes with frequent correction, reduced use or greater crowd obstruction. Treat differences as provisional because visitors and fair activity will vary between periods.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep a few seats genuinely available through voluntary turnover
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is protecting access to scarce seating by encouraging brief, renewable rests when demand is high. Set up the tent with existing seats and an unobstructed entrance. Signs say: “Rest here — everyone welcome. When others are waiting, please consider sharing a seat after a short break. Stay longer if you need.” Visitors choose whether to enter, leave or continue resting; volunteers do not assess need, enforce time limits or collect diagnoses.

One volunteer welcomes visitors and explains seat availability. The second watches for waiting visitors and crowd spillover. When seats are full, give a general, occasional reminder to the whole tent, without singling anyone out. Offer waiting visitors clear information and invite them to return; do not form a queue across a walkway. Never exceed the tent’s safe capacity.

This approach assumes seats sometimes remain occupied after visitors feel ready to move on and that a courteous prompt can release them. It cannot create capacity when everyone still needs their seat. Its principal risk is making visitors feel hurried, so comfort and freedom to stay are essential checks.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across both afternoons, alternate comparable periods with a simple open-rest welcome and with the voluntary sharing message. Keep seating, location and quiet expectations constant. Record anonymous entries, occupied-seat snapshots, people who approach but cannot find a seat, waiting groups obstructing circulation, and volunteer minutes spent explaining or prompting. Ask willing departing visitors: “Did you feel free to stay as long as you needed?” Stop prompting if visitors report pressure. The mechanism fails if seat access does not improve, waiting merely shifts outside the tent, or visitors feel hurried. Compare both afternoons and note event changes; increased turnover alone does not establish a better quiet space.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Create quieter intervals by reducing sound at its source
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is temporarily reducing nearby amplified sound so the tent offers actual acoustic relief. A tent provides little sound insulation; cooperation from the nearest sound source could therefore matter more than changes inside it.

Use the site plan to identify the tent location and nearby amplified activities. Before the trial, ask organizers whether existing sound operators can provide agreed lower-volume intervals during both afternoons, without adding staff. This alternative requires a controllable sound source, operator cooperation and permission; if these are unavailable, it is not feasible within the resources.

Keep the tent open throughout, with existing seating, a clear accessible entrance and space beside seats for mobility devices or companions. Paper signs read: “Quiet rest — everyone welcome. Come and go freely. No explanation needed.” A second sign lists agreed quieter intervals while explaining that fair sounds remain audible. Visitors can use the space outside those intervals too. Nobody is classified by disability or asked for a diagnosis.

One volunteer supports access and observes use; the other watches the approach and records crowd interference. Existing sound operators make only the agreed adjustments as part of their normal duties. Reduced sound may benefit surrounding visitors as well, but quieter intervals could attract enough demand to overwhelm the tent. Uncontrolled music, generators or traffic may also erase the benefit.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
On each afternoon, compare equal ordinary-volume and agreed lower-volume periods with the same tent layout, signs and seating. Reverse their order on the second afternoon and, where possible, compare periods within the same performance. Record anonymous entry totals, occupied-seat snapshots, blocked-path observations, and volunteer minutes spent assisting or managing spillover. Separately record coordination time. Ask willing departing visitors: “Could you get a restful break?” Record only answer totals.

The mechanism lacks support if lower-volume periods do not improve reported rest, or if crowd spillover and volunteer effort make the benefit impractical. Note performance, weather and attendance differences; two afternoons provide a feasibility check, not reliable causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make the quiet break predictable and self-directed
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is reducing uncertainty and social demands: visitors can understand how to use the tent before entering, without negotiating with a volunteer. This could make a short rest easier for anyone who feels overwhelmed, tired or reluctant to ask for help.

Use paper signs to show a simple seating diagram and explain what happens inside: “Quiet break — everyone welcome. Choose any available place. No check-in or conversation needed. Come and go freely. Fair sounds remain audible.” Mark the entrance and exit on the diagram, using the same opening if necessary. Include “For help, approach either volunteer.” Use large, plain lettering and a few simple symbols.

Arrange existing seats with a clear passage and room for someone using a mobility device to rest beside a companion. Both volunteers remain available near the edge without routinely greeting or questioning entrants; one watches access while the other observes use. They intervene when assistance or safe circulation requires it. No diagnoses or reasons for visiting are requested.

This requires a layout that can be accurately described and signs readable from the approach without blocking it. It assumes uncertainty or expected interaction deters some visitors. Written information will not serve everyone, so quiet verbal help remains available. Predictability cannot overcome dominant fair noise or insufficient seating.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
During each of two afternoons, compare equal periods with a basic “Quiet rest — everyone welcome” sign against periods adding the diagram and explicit self-service information. Reverse the order on afternoon two. Keep seating, quiet expectations and volunteer behavior constant; assume an ordinary clock is available.

Use paper tallies for entries, occupied-seat snapshots, approach obstructions, requests for procedural explanation and volunteer minutes spent assisting or managing spillover. Ask willing departing visitors: “Was it clear how to use this space?” Record answer totals only.

The mechanism is weakened if clarity does not improve or explanation requests remain similar. Reject the arrangement if sign-reading groups obstruct access or volunteer effort rises without a useful improvement in use. Note weather and nearby event changes; two afternoons establish feasibility, not a reliable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Make the quiet space discoverable before visitors need it
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is reducing search effort: a useful quiet tent can remain unused when visitors cannot locate it without asking someone. Use the existing site plan to choose two permitted decision points on established routes. Put paper signs there saying “Quiet rest tent — everyone welcome,” with accurate arrows and a simple landmark. At the tent, repeat the same wording. Avoid disability symbols or eligibility language.

Keep the tent in a reasonably quiet permitted location, with existing seating, a clear accessible entrance and a simple request to pause conversation and phone audio. Entry is voluntary; nobody explains their visit. One volunteer checks that directions remain visible and accurate and keeps the approach clear. The other supports the tent and observes use. Neither recruits passersby or records personal information.

This requires permission to display paper signs beyond the tent and a route that visitors can follow without crossing queues or hazards. If no suitable sign locations exist, this route is not viable. Direction signs cannot compensate for a noisy tent, and increased discovery may exceed its capacity. When full, volunteers state that seating is currently occupied without creating a waiting line or judging anyone’s need. Unlike changing the tent’s orientation, this proposal changes whether visitors can find the relief already available.
EXPAND.experiment: The two volunteers own a trial across both afternoons. Alternate comparable periods with entrance signage alone and with the additional direction signs, reversing the order on afternoon two. Keep tent layout and quiet expectations constant. Use paper tallies for entries, occupied-seat snapshots, requests for directions, blocked approaches and volunteer effort in fixed observation intervals. Offer departing visitors one optional question: “Was finding this space easy?” Record nearby event changes. Remove an individual direction sign immediately if it sends people into congestion; stop the added-sign condition if safe access cannot be maintained. Reject the mechanism if discovery and useful occupancy show no improvement over entrance-only signage, or if extra traffic, crowd spillover or sign maintenance outweighs the benefit. Two afternoons provide a provisional comparison, not a reliable estimate of demand.

EXPAND.title: Let visitors take a quiet break without a social checkpoint
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is removing the perceived need to request entry or engage with a greeter. Work backward from the desired outcome: someone needs to find a seat, understand the basic expectations and rest; an introductory conversation is unnecessary. At the entrance, post: “Quiet rest — everyone welcome. Walk in and choose an available seat. No check-in or conversation needed. Leave whenever you wish. Please pause conversations and phone audio.” Add “Help is available from either volunteer.”

Use the tent and existing seating in a reasonably quiet permitted location, keeping clear circulation and the exit visible. Place volunteers beside the tent rather than across its entrance. They remain available, respond to requests and address blocked access or immediate hazards, but do not initiate a welcome with every arrival. No diagnoses, names or explanations are requested. Visitors may communicate or make involuntary sounds without correction.

One volunteer owns support inside the tent; the other watches the approach and available capacity. If seats are occupied, visitors receive factual information without enforced turnover or a walkway queue. Volunteers assist anyone who appears unsure, while accepting a declined offer. This assumes the signs are understandable to many visitors; spoken help remains available when reading is difficult. The main risk is that reduced greeting feels like absence of support. Compared with the prior shared-quiet agreement, the new causal lever is removing an interpersonal entry step while retaining the same behavior expectations.
EXPAND.experiment: Across both afternoons, compare short, matched periods of a brief optional volunteer greeting with periods of self-directed entry. Reverse their order on the second afternoon. Keep signs, location, seats and quiet expectations identical. The two volunteers tally entries, approaches followed by departure before entry, requests for help, occupied-seat snapshots, crowd spillover and intervals spent actively assisting. Ask willing departing visitors: “Was it clear how to use the space and get help?” Do not infer why someone turned away. Stop the self-directed condition if repeated confusion prevents access, support requests go unanswered or circulation becomes unsafe; resume active assistance. The proposal fails if it produces no improvement in comfortable use or volunteer effort, or if any reduction in conversation comes with greater confusion or unmet support needs. Record changing fair conditions and treat the comparison as exploratory.

EXPAND.title: Choose the quietest usable position, with a practical fallback
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the sheltered-placement route by making acoustic suitability an operating decision. Before opening, one volunteer checks the site plan for permitted positions away from speakers and queues; both briefly compare those positions while fair activity is underway. Choose the quieter position only if it also has visible, accessible access and safe circulation. Orient the entrance away from passing crowds and use existing seats with clear turning space. Signs read: “Quiet rest — everyone welcome. Come and go freely.” No explanation or diagnosis is requested.

The changed action is a check when nearby amplified activity starts: the approach volunteer checks whether sound now dominates the seating area. If it does, offer visitors factual information and identify a previously checked alternative. Move only after occupants leave voluntarily and only if both volunteers can safely move the equipment; otherwise retain the seating and change the sign to “Rest space — nearby music may be audible.” Never promise acoustic relief the tent cannot provide. One volunteer remains responsible for occupants while the other checks the approach; checking stops whenever assistance is needed.

This preserves placement as the mechanism while addressing changing sound conditions. It requires permission for any alternative position and a tent that the two volunteers can handle safely. Compared with fixed placement, it may preserve useful relief but adds checking and possible setup work. If no quieter accessible position exists, paper signs and a tent cannot solve the acoustic problem.
EXPAND.experiment: Over both afternoons, compare matched periods at the ordinary feasible position and the checked sheltered position, reversing order on afternoon two where safe. Reconfigure only while empty; omit a comparison if moving is impractical. The volunteers record anonymous entries, occupied-seat snapshots, approach obstructions or waiting spillover, and active volunteer minutes, including checks and moves. Ask willing departing visitors whether the space provided relief. Record nearby performances and weather. Stop using a position if access becomes unsafe; revert to the previously safe position. Retain the checked placement only if relief improves without unacceptable spillover or effort. Two afternoons provide provisional evidence, particularly if sound conditions differ.

EXPAND.title: Give the shared quiet agreement a low-conflict recovery procedure
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the shared-behavior route by specifying what volunteers do when a reminder does not resolve deliberate conversation or phone audio. Use existing seating with clear circulation, and signs reading: “Quiet break — everyone welcome. Please pause conversations and phone audio. No explanation needed.” Entry and departure remain voluntary, and involuntary sounds or communication needed for assistance are welcome.

One volunteer supports the tent; the other monitors the approach. Before opening, the approach volunteer uses the site plan and an on-site look to identify a nearby place where a conversation could continue without blocking circulation or disturbing the tent. After one discreet reminder about conversation or phone audio, offer that location as an option. If the visitor declines, do not repeat corrections or argue. The tent volunteer offers other occupants available seats farther from the disturbance and states honestly that quiet cannot currently be assured. If no suitable nearby location exists, ask only whether audio can be paused; do not displace a group into the entrance.

The changed action closes the unresolved-reminder gap without assigning volunteers enforcement authority. It assumes most visitors will cooperate and that some disturbances can be resolved through a practical alternative. Compared with reminders alone, it may reduce repeated correction, but could transfer noise or crowds elsewhere. No additional staff, equipment, eligibility checks or enforced time limits are used.
EXPAND.experiment: Across both afternoons, alternate comparable periods of the original quiet agreement with periods using the additional recovery procedure; reverse order on afternoon two. Keep location, seats and signs constant. Volunteers tally entries, occupied-seat snapshots, unresolved conversation or phone-audio episodes, crowd spillover at both the entrance and suggested conversation location, reminder counts and active volunteer minutes. Ask willing departing visitors whether they could rest comfortably and whether reminders felt intrusive. Stop suggesting a location immediately if it obstructs circulation or disturbs nearby activity; return to a single reminder and factual assistance. Adopt the procedure only if comfortable use improves without transferring congestion or increasing correction work. Sparse disturbance episodes may leave the result inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: Make a quiet break possible without facing strangers
EXPAND.proposal:
The new mechanism is reducing social exposure within the tent. Quiet seating can still feel demanding when visitors must sit facing unfamiliar people or appear available for conversation. Arrange existing seats mainly in parallel or staggered positions rather than a face-to-face circle, with a few adjacent seats for companions. Preserve usable wheelchair spaces alongside seats, clear circulation and a visible exit. Do not reduce safe capacity simply to achieve symmetry.

A paper sign reads: “Quiet rest — everyone welcome. Sit together or take a seat on your own. Conversation is optional; please pause phone audio.” Visitors choose freely without explaining their needs. One volunteer supports occupants from beside the entrance; the second keeps the approach clear. Neither allocates seats by perceived disability or separates companions.

Before opening, the approach volunteer inspects the arrangement from seated and standing positions. If avoiding face-to-face seating blocks access, hides someone needing help or materially reduces capacity, restore the ordinary safe layout. This tests whether quiet rest requires a shared social seating arrangement at all. Compared with an ordinary conversational cluster, reduced face-to-face exposure may make resting easier, but it could feel less welcoming or accommodate fewer groups. The benefit is uncertain and depends on the tent dimensions and existing seats.
EXPAND.experiment: On each of two afternoons, compare matched periods using an ordinary seating cluster and the parallel or staggered layout, reversing their order on afternoon two. Keep tent position, seat count where feasible, signs and volunteer greeting practice constant. Change layouts only when empty. Volunteers record entries, occupied-seat snapshots, visitors unable to find suitable seating, crowd spillover and active assistance or rearrangement minutes. Ask willing departing visitors: “Could you rest comfortably without feeling you needed to interact?” Stop the alternative layout if circulation, visibility or companion access becomes difficult, and restore the safe cluster. Keep it only if reported comfort improves without a consequential loss of usable capacity or increased waiting and volunteer work. Do not infer comfort or disability from seat choices.
